 Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,
closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 4:00 pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be
summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be
recorded for public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment
due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to

  3
 adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

Reports And Comments From City Officials

During this time, members of the City Council will report on matters pertaining to their service
on various intergovernmental boards and commissions as a representative of the City
pursuant to Assembly Bill 1234. City Council Members will also have an opportunity to
comment on matters not on the agenda.

Consent Calendar Items

Agenda Items 5, 6, 7, and 8 are Consent Calendar Items. All items including Ordinances,
Resolutions and Contracts, may be approved by adoption of the Consent Calendar,
individually and collectively by one (1) motion. There will be no separate discussion of these
items unless Members of the City Council, the public, or staff request that specific items be
removed from the Consent Calendar for separate discussion and action. Members of the
public are permitted to speak on any item listed but their time period is limited to three (3)
minutes in total.

Any motion to introduce or adopt an Ordinance on the Consent Calendar shall be: (1) a
motion to waive the reading of the Ordinance and introduce the Ordinance or (2) a motion to
waive the reading of the Ordinance and adopt the Ordinance, as appropriate.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &

  6
 Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

SUBJECT:  ORDINANCE  GRANTING  A  FRANCHISE  AGREEMENT  TO
TORRANCE  PIPELINE  COMP  ANY,  LLC

PURPOSE:  The City  regulates  utility  companies  with  facilities  located  within  the public  right-
of-way  through  franchise  agreements.  On March  24, 2026,  the City  Council  adopted  Resolution
No. 2026-13-CC  declaring  its intention  to grant a franchise  to Torrance  Pipeline  Company,  LLC
(TPC)  for  the  continued  operation  of its  existing  oil  transmission  pipeline  within  the  City's
public  right-of-way.  Introduction  of the proposed  Ordinance  is the second  of three required  City
Council  actions  necessary  to grant the Franchise  Agreement  to TPC.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  Following  the  conclusion  of the  public  hearing,  the  City
Council  will  consider  waiving  the reading  in full  and introducing  an Ordinance  granting  a five-
year franchise  agreement  to Torrance  Pipeline  Company,  LLC,  for the use, maintenance,  repair,
and replacement  of one existing  pipeline  beneath  specified  public  streets,  together  with  related
appurtenances,  for the transmission  and distribution  of oil and oil products.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no impact  to the General  Fund.  If the City  Council  adopts  the
Ordinance  granting  the franchise,  Torrance  Pipeline  Company,  LLC  (TPC)  will  pay the City  a
one-time  granting  fee and ongoing  annual  franchise  fees.  Staff  recommend  a five-year  flat  fee
structure  based on the cumulative  Consumer  Price Index  for All  Urban  Consumers  (CPI-U)  over
the prior  five  years,  with  adjustments  every  five  years.  Beginning  in Year  6, the annual  fee will
be recalculated  using  the cumulative  CPI-U  from  Years  1 to 5 and then  remain  fixed  through
Year 10.

  Year  1  $38,766  $13,849  $52,615
  Year  2 to 5  $155,062  $0  $155,062

  Total  $397,348  $13,849  $411,197

The  granting  fee is consistent  with  South  Gate Municipal  Code  Title  13, Division  1, Chapter
13.10,  Section  13.10.010  (Rates  -  General).  The  annual  franchise  fee  is  established  in
compliance  with  California  Public  Utilities  Code  Section  6231.5(e)(2)  for non-publicly  owned

  1  8
 utility  pipelines.  This  statute  authorizes  an annual  franchise  fee either  (Alt  No. 1) in an amount
agreed  upon  by the applicant  and the municipality,  or (Alt  No. 2) in an amount  calculated  using
the statutory  diameter-and-length  formula.  Considering  CPI-U  inflation  and the City's  ongoing
administrative  and public  right-of-way  oversight  responsibilities  associated  with  the pipeline,  the
proposed  fees were selected  under  Alt No. 1.

NOTICING  PROCEDURE:  Before  the  City  Council  may  grant  a Franchise  Agreement,
California  Public  Utilities  Code  Sections  6232  et seq. require  the  City  to  conduct  a public
hearing.  A Notice  of Public  Hearing  was duly  published  in The  Press,  a newspaper  of general
circulation,  on April  23, 2026.

ANALYSIS:  On  October  25,  2022,  the  City  Council  adopted  Ordinance  No.  2022-09-CC
granting  Torrance  Pipeline  Company,  LLC  (TPC)  a Franchise  Agreement  to  maintain  and
operate  Pipeline  No.  M-145.  The pipeline  consists  of approximately  1.7 miles  (8,960  feet)  of
active  12-inch-diameter  pipe  and is the only  active  TPC-owned  line within  the City.  Ordinance
No.  2022-09-CC  expires  on September  13,  2026.  The  proposed  Franchise  Agreement  would
renew  the authorization  for  a 10-year  term  beginning  September  13, 2026,  through  September
13, 2036.

The proposed  Franchise  Agreement  is substantially  the same as the current  agreement,  except  for
the effective  period,  term,  and fees. Key provisions  include:

  *  AIO-yeartermfromSeptemberl3,2026toSeptemberl3,2036.

  @  Terms  and conditions  consistent  with  California  Public  Utilities  Code  Section  6201  and
  the Ordinance.

  *  Pipeline  maintenance  in compliance  with  all  applicable  city,  county,  state,  and federal
  laws, regulations,  and requirements

  *  Liability  insurance,  bonding,  and indemnification  requirements.

  *  Franchise  payments  and operating  requirements  governing  TPC's  use of the public  right-
  of-way.

  *  A  comprehensive  emergency  response  plan  meeting  federal  and  state  requirements,
  including  24-hour  notification  and  emergency  response  services  (traffic  control,
  excavation,  repair,  and necessary  supplies/services)  within  two  (2) hours  of notice,  and
  restoration  of public  streets,  alleys,  or parkways  within  seventy-two  (72) hours.

The Pipeline  is located  within  500 feet of the East Los Angeles  Community  College  expansion
project,  Southeast  High  School,  and  Simon  Rodia  Continuation  School.  The  Franchise
Agreement  requires  TPC  to operate  the Pipeline  in accordance  with  Government  Code  Section
51010,  under  which  the  California  State  Fire  Marshal  has  exclusive  safety  regulatory  and
enforcement  authority  over hazardous  liquid  pipelines.  The  State Fire  Marshal  may  implement

  2  9
 the federal  Hazardous  Liquid  Pipeline  Safety  Act  (49 U.S.C.  Sec. 2001  et seq.)  and related
federal  pipeline  safety  regulations  as needed to maintain  annual  federal  certification.

Accordingly,  the Pipeline  must  be used,  operated,  repaired,  and modified  in compliance  with
safety  regulations  established  by the California  State Fire  Marshal  and, as applicable,  the fire
authority  having  jurisdiction,  consistent  with  Chapter  13.14  (Special  Provisions  for  Oil
Pipelines),  Division  1 (Oil,  Gas and Water  Pipelines),  Title  13 (Franchises)  of the South  Gate
Municipal  Code.  The  State Fire  Marshal  is also required  to conduct  annual  inspections  of the
Pipeline  to verify  compliance,  and TPC must submit  certified  test results  pursuant  to the Pipeline
Safety  Act of 1981.

BACKGROUND:  On April  14, 2026,  the City  Council  adopted  Resolution  No.  2026-13-CC
declaring  the  City's  intention  to  grant  a franchise  to  Torrance  Pipeline  Company,  LLC,  a
Delaware  limited  liability  company,  for the continued  operation  of an existing  oil transmission
pipeline  within  the City.  Introduction  of the proposed  Ordinance  is the second  of three  required
City  Council  actions  necessary  to grant the Franchise  Agreement.

Pipeline  No.  M-145  transports  refined  oil products  from  the Torrance  Refinery  to the Vernon
Terminal  through  the City  of South  Gate. Within  the City,  the pipeline  is located  beneath  Santa
Fe Avenue  from  Independence  Avenue  to Southern  Avenue,  Southern  Avenue  from  Santa  Fe
Avenue  to Alameda  Street,  and Alameda  Street  from  Southern  Avenue  to Seminole  Avenue,
forming  one continuous  pipeline  alignment.

The proposed  schedule  for issuance  of the Franchise  Agreement  is as follows:

  1.  April  14, 2026  - The  City  Council  adopted  Resolution  No.  2026-13-CC  declaring  the
  City's  intention  to grant a franchise  agreement  to TPC.
  2.  May  12, 2026  - The City  Council  will  conduct  the required  public  hearing  and consider
  introducing  an Ordinance  granting  the franchise  to TPC.  At the conclusion  of the public
  hearing,  the City  Council  may  overmle,  deny,  or deem  insufficient  any written  protests
  and may proceed  with  granting  the franchise.
  3.  May  26, 2026  -  The  City  Council  will  consider  adopting  the  Ordinance  granting  the
  franchise  to TPC.

TPC  is requesting  renewal  of the  franchise  for  Pipeline  No.  M-145  (Ordinance  No.  2329).
Approval  is recommended  for the following  reasons:

  *  Granting  the franchise  provides  the  City  with  enforceable  rights  and requires  TPC  to
  perform  specific  obligations  for the benefit  of the City  under  Article  4 (Public  Utilities
  Code Sections  6291 through  6302)  of the Franchise  Act of 1937,  including:

  o  The  City's  right  to terminate  the franchise  and/or  pursue  legal  remedies  if TPC
  fails to perform  its obligations.

  o  Compliance  with  City  ordinances  and policies  governing  the location,  use, and
  maintenance  of the pipeline  and appurtenances.

  3  10
   o  Compensation  to the City  for repairs  to public  property  made necessary  by TPC's
  operations.

  o  Indemnification  and defense  of the City  against  claims  and damages  arising  from
  TPC's operations.

  o  Removal  and relocation  of the pipeline,  at TPC's  expense,  when  required  due to
  changes  in grade, alignment,  or width  of public  streets.

  o  Notice to the City of any sale, transfer,  assignment,  or lease of the franchise  or
  rights granted under it.

  o  Posting  of financial  security  (e.g., corporate  surety  bond  or equivalent)  available
  to the City  as liquidated  damages  if TPC fails to meet franchise  requirements.

  @  The  Franchise  Agreement  requires  TPC  to  submit  aru'iual  reports  confirming  that
  operation  and maintenance  of the pipeline  comply  with  applicable  federal  and state law.
  In a letter  dated  February  10,  2026,  the Department  of Forestry  and Fire  Protection,
  Office  of the State Fire Marshal  (OSFM),  Pipeline  Safety  Division,  confirmed  that TPC
  has maintained  and operated  Pipeline  No.  M-145  (OSFM  PLID  #0205)  in compliance
  with  applicable  Jaws and regulations.  The letter  notes  that  OSFM  identified  company-
  level  program  deficiencies  in July  2023  related  to written  procedures  under  49 C.F.R.
  §195.452  and integrity  management  requirements,  and that  amended  procedures  were
  reviewed  by OSPM.  Importantly,  no violations  were  identified  for  PLID  #0205  at the
  time  of  inspection,  and  OSFM  records  indicate  the  M-145  line  was  last  internally
  inspected  on August  20, 2024.

  If approved,  the franchise  will  provide  a one-time  granting  fee and ongoing  annual  fees to
  the City.

Compliance  with  CEQA:  Pipeline  No.  M-145  is  categorically  exempt  from  the  California
Environmental  Quality  Act  (CEQA)  pursuant  to  Section  15301  of  the  CEQA  Guidelines
(Existing  Facilities).  This  exemption  applies  because  the proposed  action  involves  continued
operation  of an existing  pipeline  franchise  with  negligible  or no expansion  of the existing  use.

with  related  appurtenances,  for transmitting  and distributing  oil and oil products.

NOW,  THEREFORE,  THE  CITY  COUNCIL  OF  THE  CITY  OF  SOUTH  GATE,
CALIFORNIA,  DOES  HEREBY  ORDAIN  AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION  1:  Definitions.  Whenever  in this Ordinance  the words  or phrases  hereinafter  in this
section  defined  are used, it is intended  that they  shall  have the respective  meanings  assigned  to
them in the following  definitions  (unless,  in the given  instance,  the context  wherein  they are used
shall clearly  import  a different  meaning):

  A)  The word "City"  shall mean the City  of South  Gate, a municipal  corporation  of the State
  of California,  in its present  incorporated  form  or in any later  reorganized,  consolidated,
  enlarged  or reincorporated  form.

SECTION  2: Grant  of Franchise.  Pursuant  to California  state law as codified  in Sections  6231
through  6235,  inclusive,  of the Public  Utilities  Code, the City  hereby  grants  to Grantee  the right,
privilege  and franchise  to operate,  maintain,  use, repair,  replace,  and remove  the Pipeline  and
Appurtenances  for  the purpose  of conducting,  transporting,  conveying  and  carrying  oil,  gas,
gasoline,  petroleum,  wet  gas, hydrocarbon  substances,  and similar  liquid  substances  under  and
across  those  portions  of the Streets  identified  in Section  1.E above  ("Franchise").  The rights
granted  herein  shall be subject  to (a) the terms  and conditions  set forth  in this Ordinance,  and (b)
repairs  to or replacements  of the Pipeline  and Appurtenances  by the Grantee,  at the Grantee's
expense,  and at such time  or times  as directed  by the City.  Grantee  shall file with  the South  Gate
City  Clerk,  not later than the Effective  Date,  a written  acceptance  of the terms  and conditions  of
this Ordinance.

SECTION  3: Term.  The Franchise  shall be for a term commencing  on September  14, 2026 and
expiring  on the tenth (lOIh) aru'iiversary  of the Effective  Date, unless terminated  earlier  by the City
pursuant  to Section  11 below.

 SECTION  4:  Fees.  As consideration  for the Franchise,  Grantee  shall pay the City  as follows:

  A)  Grantee  shall pay the City  a one-time  firanchise  granting  fee of Thirteen  Thousand  Eight
  Hundred  Forty-Nine  Dollars  ($13,849)  pursuant  to Section  13.10.010  of the South  Gate

  B)  The Grantee  shall pay the City  an annual  franchise  fee of Four  Dollars  and Thirty-Three
  Cents ($4.33) per linear  foot of the Pipeline,  which  equates to a total  annual  franchise  fee
  of  Thirty-Eight  Thousand  Seven  Hundred  Sixty-Five  Dollars  ($38,765).  The  annual
  franchise  fee shall remain  fixed  during  the initial  five  years of the term  of the Franchise.
  Upon  the sixth  (6Ih) year of the term of the Franchise,  the City  shall  adjust  the annual
  franchise  fee by applying  the cumulative  percentage  change  in the Consumer  Price  Index
  for All  Urban  Consiuners  (CPI-U)  CPI-U  (Los Angeles-Long  Beach-Anaheim  Area)  over
  the immediately  preceding  five-year  period,  and the adjusted  annual  franchise  fee shall
  remain  fixed  for the remaining  term  of the Franchise.

  C)  On or before  the Effective  Date, the Grantee  shall pay the City  an amount  equal to the  sum

  of: (i) the franchise  granting  fee; and (ii) the annual  franchise  fee for the one-year  period
  cornrnencing  on the Effective  Date.

  D)  Thereafter,  on each anniversary  of the Effective  Date  for the duration  of the term  of the
  Franchise,  Grantee  shall pay the aru'iual franchise  fee to the City.

  E)  Pursuant  to Section  13.10.060  of the South  Gate Municipal  Code,  Grantee  shall pay a late
  fee equal to ten percent  (10%)  of any payment  due hereunder,  where  such payment  remains
  unpaid  beyond  thirty  (30) days after the date on which  such payment  is due.

  F)  Any  neglect,  omission  or refusal  by the Grantee  to make  any such payment  as and when
  due shall  be grounds  for the declaration  of a forfeiture  of the Franchise  and of all rights
  hereunder  after thirty  (30) days'  notice  to cure has expired  as provided  for in Section  11
  below.

  G)  In the event of abandonment  of facilities  with  the approval  of the City  as elsewhere  in this
  Ordinance  provided,  or in the event  of removal  of such  facilities  by the Grantee,  the
  payments  otherwise  due the City  for occupancy  of the roads or highways  by such facilities
  shall be prorated  for the calendar  year in which  such removal  or abandonment  occurs  as of
  the end of the calendar  month  in which  removed  or abandoned.

permit  for the repair,  modification  or replacement  of a pipeline  for the transmission  of flammable
or combustible  liquids,  gases or hazardous  materials,  shall be as prescribed  by the Fire  Chief  of
the Los  Angeles  County  Fire  Department  in accordance  with  Chapter  13.14  of the South  Gate
Municipal  Code.

  A)  Where  it is necessary  to lay underground  pipes through,  under  or across  any portion  of a

  macadamized  street.  If the same cannot  be done,  or if it is necessary  to cut the street in
  order to access existing  pipes  and appurtenances,  such work  shall be done pursuant  to an
  excavation  permit,  as provided  in this  Section  8, to be issued  by the City  Engineer  upon

  equipment  in accordance  with  City  ordinances,  rules or regulations,  and shall comply  with
  such additional  safety  measures  as the City  Engineer  may  direct.

SECTION  9:  Emergency  Procedures

  A)  Grantee  shall  develop  and maintain  an emergency  response  plan,  satisfactory  to the City
  Engineer,  which  covers  all franchise  operations  within  the City.  The initial  draft  of that
  emergency  response  plan shall be delivered  to the City Engineer  not later than the Effective
  Date.  In general,  an emergency  response  plan  meeting  the requirements  of Federal  and
  State law and containing  the information  contained  in this section  shall be acceptable.  The

   emergency  response  plan  shall  include  a 24-hour  notification  program  and  proof  of
  arrangements  capable  of providing  emergency  response  services,  including  but not limited
  to traffic  control,  street excavation,  pipeline  repair,  and supplies  and services  as necessary,
  within  two (2) hours  of notification  of any problem,  and such other information  as the City
  Engineer  shall  reasonably  require.  Repairs  to a public  street,  alley  or parkway  shall  be
  completed  within  seventy-two  (72) hours unless otherwise  authorized  by the City Engineer.
  The City  Engineer  shall  be notified  ten (10) days in advance  of any proposed  change  in
  such arrangements.

  B)  Whenever  any Pipeline  or Appurtenance  breaks  or leaks so as to cause the release  of oil or
  products  thereof  into  the public  right-of-way,  Grantee,  and any  other  person  using  or
  controlling  the  Pipeline  or Appurtenance,  shall  immediately  notify  the  City's  Police
  Department  and  Public  Works  Department  and  shall  implement  precautionag  safety
  measures  including  traffic  control,  system  shutdown,  valve  closures,  and  public
  notification.  In the event of an emergency  which  threatens  life,  health,  safety  or property,
  and where  it is not possible  to obtain  an excavation  permit  prior  to commencement  of the
  work,  the Grantee  may commence  such work;  provided,  however,  that within  seventy-two
  (72) hours thereafter  Grantee  shall make application  to the City Engineer  for an excavation
  permit  in accordance  with  the procedures  specified  herein.  The City Engineer  may impose
  conditions  upon  the issuance  of the excavation  permit,  and all work  shall  be subject  to
  inspection.  Adequate  traffic  safety  barriers  shall  be maintained  at all times,  and any
  damaged  portion  of the Street shall be restored  to its original  condition.

  C)  If  any  portion  of  any  Street  is  damaged  by  reason  of  defects  in  the  Pipeline  and
  Appurtenances,  or any portion  thereof,  or by reason  of any other  cause attributable  to or
  arising  from  the operation  of the Pipeline  and Appurtenances,  the Grantee  shall,  at its sole
  cost and expense,  irnrnediately  repair  all damages  and restore  the Street to the condition
  existing  before  such damage  occurred.  All  such work  shall be done under the direction  of
  the City  Engineer,  and to the reasonable  satisfaction  of the City  Engineer.  Grantee  shall
  repair  such  damage  and restore  the  Street  within  three  (3) working  days  after  written
  demand  therefore  by the City  Engineer,  or such other  period  as the City  Engineer  may
  authorize  when required  for the protection  of the public  health  and safety.

  D)  If Grantee,  after reasonable  notice,  fails or refuses to pave, surface,  grade, repave,  resurface

  be done and shall keep an itemized  account  of all costs, including  reasonable  administrative
  overhead  expenses.  Grantee  shall  pay  such costs  to City  within  thirty  (30)  days  after
  presentation  to Grantee  of an itemized  account  of such costs.

SUBJECT:  APPEAL  OF  DIRECTOR  DETERMINATION  OF  THE  LAND  USE
CLASSIFICATION  FOR  A  PROPOSED  SELF-SERVICE  LAUNDROMAT  AT  4382-4390
TWEEDY  BOULEVARD;  APPELLANT:  EMILIA  KEUSHKERIAN  - (PL  N0.  26-0107)

PURPOSE:  To  consider  an  appeal  filed  by  Emilia  Keushkerian  (Appellant)  of  the  Community
Development  Director's  land  use classification  determination  for  a proposed  self-service  laundromat  at
4382-4390  Tweedy  Boulevard.  The Planning  Cornrnission  did not grant the appeal  on a tie 2-2 vote  on
April  7, 2026.

RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  Staff recommends  that the City  Council:

  1.  Considertheapplicant'sappealanddetermineiftheproposedself-servicelaundromatat4382-4390
  Tweedy  Boulevard  is most appropriately  classified  as "Personal  Services,  General"  under  South Gate
  Municipal  Code  Section  11.60,  and that  such use is a permitted  use within  the TMU-2  (Tweedy
  Mixed-Use  2) zone  pursuant  to the  Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan  land  use table.  A draft
  Resolution  denying  the appeal  has been prepared  consistent  with  the Director's  original  land use
  determination.  If the City  Council  elects to grant the appeal,  staff will  return  with  a corresponding
  resolution  at a subsequent  meeting.  An alternate  resolution  granting  the appeal  based on findings
  presented  by the appellant  is included  as an attachment  to the agenda bill.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no direct  fiscal  impact  associated  with  approval  of the appeal.

BACKGROUND:

Proiect Description
Daniel  Leal  (Applicant)  proposes  to operate  a fully  self-service  coin-operated  laundromat  at 4382,  4386,
and 4390 Tweedy  Boulevard  (collectively,  the Project  Site), encompassing  approximately  7,000 square feet
of ground-floor  commercial  space in the TMU-2  zone of the Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan. The proposed
facility  would  consist  of commercial-grade  washers  and dryers  operated  directly  by customers,  staffed
attendants  for  customer  service  and  facility  maintenance,  accessory  retail  sales  of  laundry  products
(detergent,  fabric  softener,  dryer  sheets),  and no drop-off  or pick-up  laundry  service.  Customers  bring  their
own items,  operate  machines  themselves,  and take finished  laundry  at the time  of service.  The facility  is
proposed  to serve an estimated  700 to 1,000  customer  visits  per week,  with  typical  customer  dwell  times  of

  f 26
 60 to 90 minutes.

Site and Zoning  Context
The project  site consists  of three  contiguous  storefronts  on the south  side of Tweedy  Boulevard  that are
currently  vacant.  The tenant  spaces were previously  occupied  by the Children's  Counseling  Center,  Casa
de Vape,  Sixthstar  Computers,  Cyber  Cafi:,  and Peter Pan Hair  Salon.  The property  is located  within  the
TMU-2  zone of the Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan (South  Gate Municipal  Code Chapter  11.28).  The site
has been  substantially  vacant  for  approximately  five  years.  Tweedy  Boulevard  is the  City's  primary
commercial  corridor,  and the Specific  Plan was adopted  to guide  mixed-use  revitalization  of the corridor
with  active  ground-floor  uses, extended  customer  dwell  times,  and pedestrian-oriented  design.  Fiesta  Coin
Laundry  is an existing  laundromat  located  at 4409  Tweedy  Boulevard,  about  250 feet from  the proposed
laundromat.

  Figure  1: Proposed  Laundromat  4382-4390  Tweedy  Boulevard

History  of the Use Classification  Issue
The  term  "laundromat"  does not  appear  in the current  South  Gate  Zoning  Code  (Title  11).  Prior  to a
comprehensive  zoning  update  in 2015,  laundromats  were explicitly  listed  as a conditionally  permitted  use
(CUP)  in applicable  commercial  zones  regardless  of size (Ordinance  1192  adopted  in 1972).  Laundry
agencies  were listed  as permitted  by right  in the previous  Zoning  Code,  but without  a definition  or a size
restriction.  The  2015  zoning  update  removed  the "laundromat"  term  from  Title  11,  and the Code  now
identifies  two related  but distinct  uses: 1) "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,  Agency"  and 2) "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,
Plant,"  without  specifically  addressing  self-service  coin-operated  laundry  facilities.

Following  pre-application  meetings  in April  and May  2025, the applicant  contends  that City  Planning  staff
confirmed  that a laundromat  would  be permitted  at the project  site with  no stated size restriction.  City  staff
disagrees  that representations  by City  staff  were  made  to the applicant  that  the laundromat  would  be a
permitted  use without  size restrictions.  The applicant  executed  a 10-year  lease (with  two  5-year  renewal
options)  for the project  site on May  2, 2025.  The  applicant  subsequently  invested  substantial  financial
resources  in pre-development  activities,  architectural  design,  and lease obligations  (base rent of $12,725.50
per month)  based on this understanding

  27
 In July 2025,  the City's  Public  Works  Department  placed  a hold  on plan  check  review  of the laundromat
pending  resolution  of a Planning  land use issue. The Cornrnunity  Development  Director  determined  that the
most applicable  land use classification  for a laundromat  under the current  Code is "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,
Agency  or Plant,"  with  the operative  distinction  being the 2,500-square-foot  threshold  separating  an Agency
from  a Plant.  Because  the proposed  laundromat  is approximately  7,000  square feet, the Director  classified
the proposed  use as a Laundry  Plant.

The Director  further  determined  that "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,  Plant"  is not a listed  permitted  use in the
Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan land use table,  and therefore,  the 7,000-square-foot  laundromat  could  not
be approved  in the  TMU-2  zone.  The  Director  offered  the  Applicant  the  opportunity  to  appeal  this
determination  to the Planning  Commission.

DISCUSSION/ANALYSIS:

Director's  Determination  and Basis  forAppeal
The  Director  determined  that  the  proposed  self-service  laundromat  is  most  similar  to  a "Dry
Cleaning/Laundry"  use, as defined  in South  Gate Municipal  Code Section  11.60.070,  which  distinguishes
between  two subcategories:

  *  :  A facility  where  materials  are dropped  off and picked  up for cleaning  service,  or cleaned
  on site through  either  conventional  laundry  or chemical  processes,  where  the facility  is less than
  2,500  square feet and no material  collected  at other dry cleaning  or laundry  agencies  are brought  for
  cleaning.
  *  : A  facility  greater  than 2,500  square  feet, or that processes  items  collected  from  other  retail
  locations,  where  clothing  and similar  items  are cleaned  through  either  conventional  laundry  or
  chemical  processes.

The Director  determined  that the "Agency"  and "Plant"  definitions  both  contemplate  that "materials  are
dropped  off and picked  up for cleaning  service  or cleaned  on site through  either  conventional  laundry  [or
chemical  processes]."  The  Director  concluded  that  the  laundromat  activities  are  within  the  Dry
Cleaning/Laundry  classification  in which  customers  utilize  laundry  appliances  on-site  for  conventional
cleaning.  Because  the proposed  laundromat  is approximately  7,000 square  feet, the Director  classified  it as
a Laundry  Plant.  The Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan  land  use table  identifies  "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,
Agency"  as a permitted  use inthe  TMU-2  zone but does not list "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,  Plant."  The Director
therefore  concluded  that the proposed  laundromat  use is permitted  at the proposed  site within  the TMU-2
zone if less than 2,500 sq. ft. in size, however  the applicant  would  not be permitted  to operate  at the proposed
7,000 sq. ft. facility  size.  The applicant  indicated  to staffthat  it is critical  to their laundromat  business  model
to operate  a facility  greater  than 2,500  sq. ft.  Staff  suspects  that the omission  of "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,
Plant"  from  the Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan land use table was intentional  to limit  the size of laundry
facilities  that could preclude  retail  and dining  establishments  along Tweedy  Boulevard,  although  this cannot
be verified  from  existing  specific  plan documentation.

The  Director  acknowledges  that  there  is  genuine  ambiguity  in  applying  the  Laundry  Agency/Plant
framework  to a self-service  coin-operated  laundromat.  The Director  has separately  briefed  the Planning
Commission  on apending  code amendment  thatwould  add "laundromat"  as an explicitly  listed  conditionally
permitted  use  in  the  Urban  Mixed-Use  zones  with  a 2,500-foot  distance  separation;  however,  that
amendment  is months  away  from  adoption.  Under  the proposed  dra'ft  code  amendment,  the proposed

  28
  3
 laundromat  would  not be permitted  due to the existing  laundromat  located  approximately  250 feet from  the
project  site.  The  Director  identified  the appeal  process  as the procedural  mechanism  available  to the
Applicant  to challenge  the land use determination.

The Applicant,  AquaLoop  Laundromat  LLC,  has appealed  the Director's  determination  on the grounds  that
a self-service  laundromat  is not properly  classified  as a Dry Cleaning/Laundry  use under  any definition  and
is more correctly  classified  as "Personal  Services,  General,"  a permitted  use by right  in the TM[J-2  zone.

Applicant's  Appeal  Justification
The  Applicant's  appeal  justification  (Attachment  3)  advances  two  primary  arguments:  (A)  the  Dry
Cleaning/Laundry  definitions  do not describe  a self-service  laundromat,  and (B) a self-service  laundromat
satisfies  the definition  of Personal  Services,  General  and is consistent  withthe  listed examples  and analogous
uses under that definition.

A. Misclassificahon  as Dry  Cleaning/Laundry  -Agency  or Plant
The Applicant  argues that both the Agency  and Plant  definitions  describe  a business  that performs  cleaning
services  on behalf  of customers.  In both  definitions,  materials  are "dropped  off  and picked  up,"  and the
business  cleans  items  through  "conventional  laundry  or  chemical  processes."  The  2,500-square-foot
threshold  was  designed  to distinguish  a small  drop-off  retail  location  (Agency)  from  a large  service-
processing  facility  (Plant),  both of which  involve  the business  performing  the cleaning.

A self-service  laundromat  fits neither  description.  No items are dropped  off. No items are picked  up by staff.
The  business  does not  perform  any cleaning.  Customers  bring  their  own  laundry,  operate  commercial
washing  and drying  machines  themselves,  and take their  items  when  the cycle  is complete.  The 2,500-
square-foot  threshold  has no logical  application  to a self-service  model,  because that threshold  was designed
to regulate  the scale of a laundry  service  processing  operation,  not the customer  capacity  of a self-service
facility.

B. Correct  Classification  as Personal  Services,  General
The Applicant  argues that the proposed  laundromat  Satisfies  each element  of the Personal  Services,  General
definition  in South  Gate Municipal  Code Section  11.60:
  *  "Personal  Services"  (land  use) means  any place of business  providing  services  and accessory  retail
  sales of products  related  to the services  provided.
  *  "General"  means establishments  providing  nonmedical  services  to individuals  as a primary  use.

The Applicant's  analysis  is as follows:

  1.  Nonrnedical  service  to individuals  as primary  use. Customers  visit  the facility  to perform  a personal
  task of washing  and drying  their  clothing  and household  textiles.  The business  provides  the service
  of making  commercial-grade  equipment  available  in a clean,  professionally  maintained,  and staffed
  environment.  This is a nonmedical  service  to individuals  as a primary  use.
  2.  Accessory  retail  sales of products  related  to the services  provided.  Laundromats  customarily  sell
  detergent,  fabric  softener,  dryer  sheets, stain removers,  and related  products,  mirroring  how a barber
  shop sells hair care products,  a tailor  sells thread  and notions,  or a fitness  center  sells supplements.
  3.  The listed  examples  are non-exhaustive.  The Code  states that general  personal  service  uses "may
  also include"  the listed  examples  (barber/beauty  shop,  clothing  rental,  home  electronics  and small
  appliance  repair,  locksmith,  pet  grooming,  shoe repair,  tailor,  waxing  shop)  and uses the term

  29
   "include,"  not "limited  to." A self-service  laundromat  is an unlisted  but quali:fying  example  under
  this non-exhaustive  framework.
  4. The fitness center analogy.  The Personal  Services  definition  already  encompasses  fitness  and health
  facilities,  defined  as any  place  of  business  providing  facilities  devoted  to health,  beauty,  and
  relaxation,  including  health  or physical  fitness  centers.  A  fitness  center  provides  commercial
  equipment  in a maintained  facility;  customers  arrive,  operate  the equipment  themselves,  remain  on-
  site for an extended  period,  and depart.  A self-service  laundromat  operates  on an identical  model
  characterized  by commercial  equipment,  self-operation  by the customer,  extended  dwell  time,  and
  no service  performed  by the operator  on the customer's  behalf.  If a facility  where  customers  use
  equipment  and leave is a personal  service  when that equipment  is a treadmill,  it is equally  a personal
  service  when that equipment  is a washing  machine.

Zoning  Code  Text Ambiguity
The Director  has acknowledged  that there  is genuine  ambiguity  in classi:tying  a self-service  laundromat
under the current  Code. The Dry Cleaning/Laundry  Agency  and Plant definitions  were drafted  for businesses
that perform  cleaning  services  for customers,  such as dry cleaners,  linen  service  providers,  and cornrnercial
laundry  operators.  These  definitions  do not capture  the self-service  model.  The applicability  of the 2,500-
square-foot  threshold  to a coin-operated  laundromat  is particularly  unclear,  as that threshold  may have been
designed  to regulate  the scale of service  processing  operations,  not the customer-facing  floor  area of a self-
service  facility.  The Director  contacted  a former  city planner  who was present  during  the 2015 zoning  code
update  to understand  the reason  for the laundromat  classification  change.  The planner  was not certain  of
the justification  for the change,  but believed  the intent  was to prohibit  laundromats  citywide  by omitting  the
land use classification  entirely.

Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan  Policy  Consistency
The proposed  laundromat  is consistent  with  the goals and policies  of the Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan.
The Specific  Plan was adoptedto  encourage  active,  pedestrian-oriented  ground-floor  uses along the corridor,
reduce  vacancy,  attract  businesses  that generate  sustained  foot traffic,  and serve the daily  needs of a dense,
renter-majority  neighborhood.  The proposed  project  would:

  *  Activate  three  contiguous  storefronts  that  have  been  substantially  vacant  for  approximately  five
  years, in a corridor  with  approximately  30 vacant  storefronts  along Tweedy  Boulevard.
  *  Generate  an estimated  700 to 1,000  customer  visits  per week,  with  60 to 90 minute  dwell  times  per
  visit,  supporting  sustained  pedestrian  activity  and ancillary  commercial  vitality.
  *  Serve an essential  daily  need for residents  in a high-density,  renter-majority  neighborhood  where  in-
  unit  laundry  is limited  and access to cornrnercial  laundry  facilities  is a significant  quality-of-life
  concern.

  *  Represent  a 10-year  lease commitment  (with  options  to extend  to 20 years),  providing  long-term
  corridor  stability  and anchoring  contiguous  storefronts  under  active  use.

  *  Be designed  as a modern,  attended  facility  with  transparent  storefront  design  and high-quality
  finishes,  consistent  with  the Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan's  design  standards  for active  ground-
  floor  commercial  uses.

  30
 CONCLUSION:

Based  on the foregoing  analysis,  staff  recornrnends  that the City  Council  consider  the applicant's  appeal
justification  that a self-service  coin-operated  laundromat,  as proposed  at 4382-4390  Tweedy  Boulevard,  is
most accurately  classified  as "Personal  Services,  General"  under South Gate Municipal  Code Section  11.60,
rather than "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,  Agency  or Plant."  The Director  has acknowledged  that there is genuine
ambiguity  in classifying  a self-service  laundromat  under  the current  Code;  however,  the Director  has not
modified  the original  land use determination.  To address  this ambiguity  prospectively,  a code amendment
to clarify  the laundromat  use classification  is currently  under  staff review  that would  allow  laundromats  at
any size, but at a separation  distance  of up to 2,500  distance  to avoid  an overconcentration  of laundromat
businesses.  Under  the current  Director's  land use determination,  the applicant  would  still be able to operate
a laundromat  of 2,500  square  feet or less in the TMU-2  zone or choose  to operate  as a permitted  use in
locations  in  the  Industrial  Flex  (IF),  Light  Industrial  (LI),  Light  Manufacturing  (M2)  or  Heavy
Manufacturing  (M3)  zoning  districts.

A City  Council  determination  to grant the appeal would  allow  the Applicant  to proceed  with  permitting  and

   Finding  A -  The  Proposed  Use Exceeds  the Size Threshold  for  a Laundry  Agency.
  The proposed  laundromat  is approximately  7,000  square  feet, which  exceeds  the 2,500
  square-foot  maximum  that  distinguishes  a Dry  Cleaning/Laundry  Agency  from  a Dry
  Cleaning/Laundry  Plant  under  South  Gate Municipal  Code  Section  11.60.070.  The  size
  threshold  established  in the Code is an objective,  quantifiable  standard.  Regardless  of the
  operational  model  of the proposed  use, the proposed  facility's  square  footage  places  it
  squarely  within  the Plant definition  under the plain  language  of the Code.

  Finding  B -  "Dry  Cleaning/Iiaundry,  Plant"  Is Not  a Permitted  Use ip the TMU-2
  . The Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan land use table for the TMU-2  zone lists "Dry
  Cleaning/Laundry,  Agency"  as a pernnitted  use, but does not list "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,
  Plant."  Because  the proposed  facility  must  be classified  as a Plant  based on its size, and
  because  a Plant  is not an identified  permitted  use in the TMU-2  zone, the proposed  use is
  not permitted  in the TMU-2  zone under  the current  land use table.

  Finding  C -  The Proposed  Use Does Not Satisfy  the Definition  of Personal  Services,
  . The Applicant  contends  that the proposed  laundromat  should  be classified  as

  examples  such  as barber/beauty  shops,  clothing  rental,  home  electronics  and  small

 NOW,  THEREFORE,  THE  CITY  COUNCIL  DOES  HEREBY  FIND,  DETERMINE  AND
DECLARE  AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION  1.  All  of the  facts  set forth  in the recitals  above  are true  and  correct  and  are
incorporated  herein  by reference.

SECTION  2.  Based  upon  substantial  evidence  presented  to the City  Council  during  the public
hearing  conducted  with  regard  to the Applicant's  appeal,  including  the written  staff report,  verbal
testimony,  and all other  evidence  in the record,  the City  Council  hereby  grants  the appeal  and
determines  that the proposed  self-service  laundromat  at 4382-4390  Tweedy  Boulevard  is most
appropriately  classified  as "Personal  Services,  General"  under  South Gate Municipal  Code Section
11.60,  which  is a permitted  use by right  in the TMU-2  zone of the Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific
Plan, based on the following  findings:

Finding  A. The Dry  Cleaning/Laundry  Agency  and Plant  Definitions  Do Not Describe  a Self-
Service  Laundromat.  Both  the "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,  Agency"  and "Dry  Cleaning/Laundry,
Plant"  definitions  in  South  Gate  Municipal  Code  Section  11.60.070  describe  businesses  that
perform  cleaning  services  on behalf  of customers,  in which  materials  are "dropped  off and picked
up" and the business  cleans the items through  "conventional  laundry  or chemical  processes."  The
proposed  facility  fits neither  description.  No items are dropped  off, no items are picked  up by staff;
and the business  does not perform  any  cleaning.  Customers  bring  their  own  laundry,  operate
commercial  washing  and drying  machines  themselves,  and remove  their  items  when  the cycle  is
complete.  The fundamental  operational  element  common  to both the Agency  and Plant  definition
of the business  performing  a cleaning  service  for the customer  is absent from  the proposed  use.

Finding  B.  The  2,500-Square-Foot  Threshold  Has No Logical  Application  to a Self-Service
Model.  The  2,500-square-foot  threshold  separating  an Agency  from  a Plant  under  Section
11.60.070  was  designed  to distinguish  a small  drop-off  retail  location  from  a large  service-
processing  facility,  both  of which  involve  the business  performing  the cleaning.  Because  that
threshold  was  directed  at the  scale  of a laundry  service-processing  operation  rather  than  the
customer  capacity  of a self-service  facility,  applying  that threshold  to a self-service  coin-operated
laundromat  does not advance  the regulatory  purpose  for which  the threshold  was created.  The
Director  has  acknowledged  that  there  is  genuine  ambiguity  in  applying  the  Agency/Plant
framework  to a self-service  laundromat,  and the City  Council  finds  that this ambiguity  must  be
resolved  in favor  of the classification  that most  accurately  describes  the actual  operation  of the
proposed  use.

Finding  C. The  Proposed  Use Satisfies  the Definition  of "Personal  Services,  General."  The
proposed  laundromat  satisfies  each element  of the "Personal  Services,  General"  definition  in South
Gate Municipal  Code  Section  11.60.  First,  customers  visit  the facility  to perform  a personal  task
of washing  and drying  their  clothing  and household  textiles,  and then the business  provides  the
service  of making  commercial-grade  equipment  available  in a clean,  professionally  maintained,
and staffed  environment,  which  constitutes  a nonmedical  service  to individuals  as a primary  use.

  t'}  39
 Second,  the proposed  accessory  retail  sales  of  detergent,  fabric  softener,  dryer  sheets,  stain
removers,  and related  products  mirror  the  accessory  retail  component  characteristic  of  other
personal service uses, such as a barber shop selling  hair care products,  a tailor  selling  thread  and
notions,  or a fitness  center  selling  supplements.  Third,  the listed  examples  of general  personal
services  in the Code are non-exhaustive,  as the Code provides  that such uses "may  also include"
the listed  examples  and uses the term "include,"  not "limited  to."

Finding  D.  The  Personal  Services  Definition  Already  Encompasses  Analogous  Self-
Operated Equipment  Uses. The "Personal  Services"  definition  already  encompasses  fitness  and
health  facilities,  including  health  or physical  fitness  centers,  where  customers  arrive,  operate
commercial  equipment  themselves,  remain  on-site  for an extended  period,  and depart  without  any

service  performed  by the operator  on the customer's  behalf.  A self-service  laundromat  operates  on
an identical  model  of commercial  equipment  self-operated  by the customer,  extended  dwell  time,
and no service  performed  by the operator  on the customer's  behalf.  The City  Council  finds  that if
a facility  where  customers  use equipment  and leave is a personal  service  when  the equipment  is a
treadmill,  it is equally  a personal  service  when the equipment  is a washing  machine.

Finding  E. The  Proposed  Use  Is  Consistent  with  the  Goals  and  Policies  of the  Tweedy
Boulevard  Specific  Plan.  The Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan was adopted  to encourage  active,
pedestrian-oriented  ground-floor  uses along  the corridor,  reduce  vacancy,  attract  businesses  that
generate  sustained  foot traffic,  and serve the daily  needs of a dense, renter-majority  neighborhood.
The proposed  laundromat  would  activate  three contiguous  storefronts  that have been substantially
vacant  for  approximately  five  years  in  a corridor  with  approximately  30 vacant  storefronts;
generate  an estimated  700 to 1,000  customer  visits  per week  with  typical  60 to 90 minute  dwell

2. The Misclassification  Problem

The City classifies the laundromat under "Dry Cleaning/Laundry"in  Section 11.60.070  of the
Zoning Code. That definition has two subcategories:

Agency - "a facility where materials are dropped off and picked up for cleaning service, or
cleaned on site through either conventional laundry or chemical processes where an agency is
less than 2,500 square feet and no material collected at other dry cleaning or laundry agencies
are brought for cleaning."

Plant - "a facility greater than 2,500 square feet or that processes items collected from other
retail locations, where clothing and similar items are cleaned through either conventional
laundry or chemical  processes."

Both definitions describe a business that performs cleaning as a service for the customer.
Materials are "dropped off and picked up." The business cleans items through "conventional
laundry or chemical processes." The 2,500 SF threshold distinguishes a small drop-off location
from a larger processing  facility.

A self-service  laundromat  does none of this. No items are "dropped off." No items are
"picked up." The business does not perform any cleaning. Customers bring their own laundry,
operate the machines themselves, and take their items when finished. The 2,500 SF threshold
has no logical application to this model because it was designed to regulate the scale of a
service processing  operation,  not the customer capacity of a self-service facility.

3. The Correct  Classification:  Personal  Services

After your March 3 meeting, Gabriel Perez emailed Emilia the Personal Services definition from
Chapter 11.60. He stated: "It was mentioned the need for the definitions of personal services."
This was a clear signal about where to anchor the appeal. The definition reads:

For more  than  three  decades,  Automated  Laundry  Systems  has designed  and developed
high-quality self-service laundromats  throughout  California,  Nevada, and Arizona.  Over that
time, we have helped bring modern,  clean, and community-focused  laundry facilities  to dozens
of neighborhoods,  often  revitalizing  underutilized  retail spaces and increasing  foot traffic for
surrounding  businesses.

We are excited  about  the opportunity  to develop  a new laundromat  at 4390  Tweedy
Boulevard,  one of South Gate's most important  commercial  corridors.  This particular  space
has remained  vacant for approximately  five years, and we see this project as an opportunity  to
bring new activity and investment  back to the property  and the surrounding  businesses.
Laundromats are also inherently long-term  neighborhood  businesses.  This location  would be
operated  by Eric Baruch, a long-time  client of ours and a committed  investor in the laundry
industry.  Laundromats  are also inherently  long-term  neighborhood  businesses.  After
conducting  our due diligence  and confirming  with the City Planning  Department  that a
laundromat is a permitted  use at this location,  we submitted  our plans for approval.  We were
therefore surprised  to learn that the project  was  being  categorized  as a "planned  facility"  with
a size limitation  of 2,500 square feet.

We respectfully  believe  this classification  does  not accurately  reflect  the nature  of a self-
service  laundromat,  which  is fundamentally  different  from  a closed-door  laundry  pickup  and
drop-off  facility.

A planned  laundry  facility  typically refers to a back-of-house  operation that functions  primarily
as a pickup and drop-off  service, similar to a dry-cleaning  plant. These facilities  do not
generate  meaningful  foot traffic or provide a gathering  space for the community.

A self-service  laundromat,  however,  is a storefront  neighborhood  amenity that actively  serves
residents  and contributes  to the vitality of a commercial  district. Customers  often spend
extended  periods of time in the area while completing  their laundry, frequently  visiting  nearby
restaurants,  coffee shops, and retail businesses.  Many families come together,  particularly  on
weekends,  and the laundromat  becomes  part of their routine within the neighborhood.

Based  on our experience  operating  similar  facilities  in communities  with  comparable
demographics,  we estimate  the location  could generate  700-1,000  customer  visits per week.
This level of consistent  foot traffic would  help support  existing  businesses  along Tweedy
Boulevard  while also making the corridor  more attractive  for new businesses  to fill currently
vacant storefronts.

During  our review  of the area, we observed  approximately  30 vacant  commercial  spaces
along Tweedy  Boulevard.  A well-designed  laundromat  can act as an anchor for neighborhood
activity by bringing  reliable, daily traffic to the street and encouraging  complementary
businesses  such as cafes, restaurants,  and small retailers to locate nearby.

The laundromat  we are proposing  would  also represent  a significant  investment  in the
neighborhood.  Automated  Laundry  Systems  is known  for building  modern,  high-quality
facilities that prioritize cleanliness,  safety, and customer  comfort.  The proposed  laundromat
would include:

needs  of the community  without  long wait times for machines
  -  State-of-the-art  Maytag  washers  and  dryers  designed  for energy  and water
efficiency
  -  A clean,  welcoming  environment  with  comfortable  seating  areas  and  ample
folding  tables
  -  High-quality  finishes  such  as stainless  steel  bulkheads  and  granite  folding
surfgces
  A fully  attended  facility,  ensuring  safety,  cleanliness,  and customer  assistance
at all times

Our goal is not simply to open another business,  but to create  a community-oriented  facility
that residents can rely on and take pride in.

We strongly  believe this project will serve the residents  of South Gate by providing  an essential
service while also supporting  economic  activity along one of the city's most important
commercial  streets.

We respectfully  request that the Planning  Commission  reconsider  the classification  of this
project and allow the proposed  laundromat  to move forward  as a self-service  retail use rather
than a "planned  facility." Doing so will allow us to deliver a high-quality  amenity that benefits
both the local community  and the surrounding  business  district.

Thank you for your time and consideration.  We would welcome  the opportunity  to answer any
questions  and further discuss how this project can positively contribute  to the South Gate
community.

Sincerely,

 Nexus Study Overview
The City commissioned the DIF Nexus Shidy. The purpose of the study was to establish the legal
and technical foundation to update the existing traffic impact fee program (formerly the Road
Mitigation  Fee Program) and to create new development impact fee programs  for Parks and
Recreation Facilities and Public Safety Facilities.

Fee Basis  and  Cost  Allocation
The Nexus Study identifies the maximum justified fee amounts that may be charged to new
development, based on the cost of facilities needed to serve future growth. These facilities are
derived from adopted planning documents and City policy, including the Capital Improvement
Plan, Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan, Hollydale Village Specific Plan, South Gate Bicycle
Transportation Plan, Southeast Gateway Line First/Last Mile Plan, and the Los Angeles River
Master Plan. Through the impact fees, new development can pay for its fair share of these
improvements, though the City must commit to fully funding existing development's share of the
identified improvements through 2050, or else new development will have paid too much.

DIF Methodology  and Cost Allocation
City staff are proposing to update the methodology  used to calculate non-residential  traffic
impact fees. Rather than relying on a building size (per square foot) model with standard trip
assumptions, the Nexus Study recommends a cost-per-trip approach, which calculates fees based
on the estimated number of trips a project is expected to generate. This method more accurately
reflects a project's actual impact on the transportation system and improves the overall fairness
and defensibility  of the fee structure.

The Nexus Study also finds that the City's current development impact fees are below the actual
cost of infrastructure needed to support new growth. Updating these fees would better align them
with the true impacts  of development.

Table 1 (Attachment B) provides examples of proposed impact fees and how they are distributed
across key service areas: traffic mitigation, parks and recreation, and public safety. These are
one-time  fees paid by new development  projects  to help fund needed infrastructure
improvements.  Below is a description of each service area's fiscal impact, along with an
explanation of how the fees are calculated based on estimated demand.

Traffic  Mitigation
  *  Calculation basis: Estimated average daily vehicle trips generated by the project.
  *  Overview: Traffic mitigation  fees typically  represent the largest cost component  for
  commercial and industrial developments due to their impact on the roadway network.
  *  Examples: A mgh-intensity logistics facility may be assessed by $6 million or more,
  while smaller commercial developments may exceed $2 million, depending on projected
  traffic generation.

Parks and Recreation
  *  Calculation  basis:  Projected  number  of  new  residents  (applicable  to  residential
  development).
  *  Overview: Residential projects contribute the most toward park and recreation  facilities
  due to increased demand from new population growth.
  *  Example:  A  100-unit  apartment  development  may  be  required  to  contribute
  approximately  $2.4 million toward park improvements.
  2  90
 Public  Safety
  *  Calculation  basis: Project  size and development  type.
  *  Overview:  Fees for police  and fire  services  are generally  lower  in comparison  to other
  categories  but are necessary  to ensure the city can maintain  adequate  service  levels.
  Typical  range:  Generally,  in the tens of thousands  of dollars  per project,  depending  on
  scale and intensity  of development.

These  factors  are multiplied  by set cost  amounts  so that  projects  that  create  more  demand  or
impact  pay a fair share toward  the infrastructure  needed to support  growth.

Non-Fee  funding  required:  If the City  adopts  the maximum  allowable  impact  fees, those  fees
will  cover  the portion  of infrastructure  costs attributed  to new development,  based on the Nexus
Study.  However,  this is not enough  to pay for all the facilities  needed.

Some  of the infrastructure  benefits  both  new  and existing  development.  The portion  that serves
existing  development-about  $284.4 million-cannot  be paid  for with  impact  fees. Instead,  the
City  must  use other  funding  sources  (such  as grants,  general  funds,  or other  revenues)  to cover
this share by 2050.  If it does not, new development  could  end up paying  more than its fair share.

Development  Fee Comparison
Below  Willdan  prepared  a comparison  of impact  fees noted  in the DIF  Nexus  Study  and nearby
cities  using  five  different  development  project  usages  with  chart  illustrations,  included  as
Attachment  C.

Residential  Fee Comparison
The first two charts,  in Attachment  C, compare  fees for residential  projects:  a single-family  home
and an 18-unit  apartment  building.  The findings  show  that South  Gate's  current  impact  fees are
lower  than  most  nearby  cities.  This  means  new  development  in South  Gate pays  less toward
infrastructure  costs  than  development  in  surrounding  areas.  The  Nexus  Study  identifies  the
highest  legally  allowed  fees, which  are higher  than  current  fees. If adopted,  these higher  fees
would  bring  South  Gate more  in line  with  neighboring  cities  and better  reflect  the real  cost of
growth  on roads,  parks,  and public  safety.  However,  the City  Council  can choose  to set fees at a
lower  level than the maximum  allowed  by law.

Non-Residential  Fee Comparison
The subsequent  three  charts  (in Attachment  C) compare  development  fees for different  types  of
projects:  10,000  square feet of retail  or commercial  space, 10,000  square feet of office  space, and
100,000  square  feet of industrial  space, across nearby  cities.  The results  show  that South  Gate's
current  fees are generally  higher  than some nearby  cities,  but still  lower  than the highest  amounts
allowed  under  the Nexus  Study.  This  means  South  Gate is somewhat  competitive  compared  to
surrounding  areas,  but  the  current  fees  still  do not  fully  cover  the  cost  of the infrastructure
needed  to  support  new  development,  especially  industrial  projects.  If  the  City  adopts  the
maximum  justified  fees, the charges  will  better  reflect  the actual  impact  that new development
has on infrastructure  such as roads, parks,  and public  safety.

However,  the  City  Council  can  still  choose  to  set fees  lower  than  the  maximum  allowed,
depending  on its policy  goals and priorities.

  3  91
 BACKGROUND:  The City  established  its Development  Impact  Fee (DIF)  Program  in 2008  in
compliance  with  Assembly  Bill  1600  (Mitigation  Fee Act),  codified  in the South  Gate Municipal
Code under  Chapter  5.35 (Road  Mitigation  Fee Program)  and Chapter  9.46.040  (DIF  Fund).  This
program  authorizes  the City  to collect  impact  fees from  new  development  to offset  the cost of
capital  facilities  and infrastructure  needed  to serve  that  growth,  consistent  with  Governrnent
Code  Sections  66000  et seq. DIFs  are an important  funding  source  used to support  ongoing  and
future  infrastructure  improvements,  particularly  for roadway  systems.

Need  for Fee Update
As development  activity  has continued,  the City  recognized  the need to update  its existing  fee
structure  and expand  the program  to address  broader  infrastructure  demands.  In response,  the
City  retained  Willdan  Group,  Inc. to prepare  a Development  Impact  Fee (DIF)  Nexus  Study.  The
purpose  of the  study  is to ensure  the  City  can legally  justify  and fairly  assess fees  on new
development  to cover its proportionate  share of impacts  to public  infrastructure

Nexus  Study  Purpose  and Scope
The Nexus  Study  provides  the legal  and technical  foundation  required  by State law to update  the
City's  traffic  impact  fee program  and to expand  the DIF  program  to include  new  fees for  (1)
parks and recreation  facilities  and (2) public  safety  facilities.  It identifies  the relationship  (nexus)
between  new development  and the need for expanded  or new public  facilities,  and calculates  the
maximum  legally  justified  fee amounts  based on planned  infrastructure  improvements  identified
in adopted  City  plans and policies.

Key  Findings
The  study  concludes  that  the  City  can  legally  establish  updated  and  expanded  development
impact  fees to help  fund  needed  traffic,  parks  and recreation,  and public  safety  improvements
driven  by new  development.  While  the Nexus  Study  establishes  the maximum  allowable  fee
levels,  the City  Council  retains  discretion  to adopt  fees at or below  those  amounts  based  on
policy  considerations,  including  the  desire  to  encourage  certain  types  of  development.  A
comparison  with  neighboring  jurisdictions  is also  included  to provide  regional  context  for the
City's  current  and proposed  fee levels.

Adoption  Requirements
Pursuant  to  State  law,  effective  Januaty  1, 2022,  a Nexus  Study  must  be adopted  prior  to
establishing  or increasing  any development  impact  fee. The study  must  be presented  at a duly
noticed  public  hearing  with  a minimum  30-day  notice  period.  Upon  City  Council  adoption,  any
approved  fees would  become  effective  60 days thereafter.

Fiscal  and Policy  Implications
Adoption  of  updated  DIFs  would  establish  a dedicated  funding  source  for  infrastructure
improvements  needed  to support  new  development,  reducing  reliance  on the General  Fund  and
other limited  resources.  It would  also ensure that new development  contributes  proportionately  to
the impacts  it generates,  improving  fairness  across  project  types  and avoiding  the transfer  of
growth-related  costs  to existing  residents.  Conversely,  without  adoption,  the City  would  face
increased  financial  pressure  to  fund  these  improvements  with  limited  resources,  potentially
affecting  service  levels  and delaying  needed  infrastructure  projects.

This report  presents  an analysis  of the need for  capital  facilities to accommodate  new
development  in the City of South  Gate. This chapter  explains  the study approach  under the
following sections:

Capital  Facilities  Financing  in California
The  changing  fiscal  landscape  in California  during  the pasf 45 years  has steadily  undercut  the
financial  capacity of local governments ta fund infrastructure.  Three  dominant  trends  stand  out,
the latter two of which have been exacerbated  duringthe  past several  years:

  The passage of a string or tag,limitation measures,  starting with Proposition  13 in
  1978 and continuing  through the passage of Proposition  218 in 1 996;

  Decliningpopularsupportfor bond measuresto financeinfrastructurefor the next
  generati6n  of residents  and businesses;  and

  Steep reductions  in federal  and state assistance.

Faced with ihese trends, many qities  and counties have for many years had to adopt a policy of
"growth pays.its own way." This.policy  shifis the burden of funding infrastructure expansion from
existing  rates and taxpayers  onto new development.  This funding shift has been  accomplished
primarily  through the imposition'  of assessments,  special taxes, and development  impact fees,
also known as public facilities.fees.  Assessments  and special  taxes require approval of property
owners  and are appropriate  when  the: funded  facilities are  directly related to the developing
property.  Development  impact fees, on the other hand, are an appropriate  funding source for
facilities that require expansion  due to the increased  demands  created by new development,  but
that also serve all' development  jurisdiction-wide  or area-wide.  Development  impact fees need
only a majority vote of'the legislative  body for adoption.

Background  and Study  Objectives
The  primary  policy  objective  of a development  impact  fee  program  is to  ensure  that  new
development  pays the capital costs associated  with growth. The primary purpose  of this report  is
to update and recalculate  and present fees that will enable the City to expand  its inventory  of
capital facilities, as new development  leads to service population increases.

This report  is an update  of the development  impact  fee (DIF) calculated  for and documented  most
recently in the development  impact fee nexus study titled: "Traffic Impact Fee Study,  City of South
Gate, July 31, 2008", by Willdan Financial  Services.  This previous study calculated  traffic impact

Fee  Program  Maintenance
Once  a fee program  has been adopted  it must be properly  maintained  to ensure  that the revenue
collected  adequately  funds the facilities  needed  by new development.  To avoid collecting
inadequate  revenue,  the inventories  of existing facilities and costs for planned facilities must be
updated periodically  for inflation, and the fees recalculated  to reflect the higher costs. The use of
established indices for each facility included in the inventories  (land, buildings,  and equipment),
such as the California Construction  Cost Index, is necessary  to accurately  adjust  the impact fees.

While  fee updates  using  inflation  indices  are appropriate  for annual  or periodic  updates  to ensure
that fee revenues  keep  up with  increases  in the costs  of public  facilities,  it is recommended  to

when significant  new data on growth forecasts  and/or facility plans become  available. For further
detail on fee program implementation,  see Chapter 7.

Administrative  Costs
Administration of an impact fee program to comply with the requirements  or the Mitigation Fee Act
imposes costs on the City for capital budgeting,  fee adjustments, mandated  annual reports and 5-
year reviews of the impact fee program,  as well as periodic impact fee update studies and legal
review. It is common practice  in California  for cities to add a small administrative  charge  to impact
fees to cover those costs.

This study uses an assumption  of 1% of the maximum justified fee to estimate  the administrative
costs associated  with the fee  program,  consistent with the last impact fee  study. This study
assumes 1 % of the maximum justified fee to estimate the administrative  costs associated  with the
fee program.  To validate this assumption,  Willdan reviewed the administrative  costs associated
with other cities in California in FY2022-23. Those costs ranged from 132%  to 1.52% of collected
impact fee  revenue  in the  other  jurisdictions.  Thus,  the  assumed  I.O%  of fee  revenue  is
conservative.

Study  Methodology
Development  impact fees are calculated  to fund  the cost or facilities required  to accommodate
growth. The six steps followed in this development  impact fee study include:

  1.  Estimate  existing  development  and  future  growth:  Identify  a base  year  for
  existing  development  and  a growth  forecast  that  reflects  increased  demand  for
  capital facilities;

  2.  Identify facility standards:  Determine  the facility  standards  used  to plan  for new
  and expanded facilities;

  3.  Determine  facilities required  to serve  new development:  Estimate  the  total
  amount of planned facilities,  and identify the share required  to accommodate  new
  development;

  4.  Determine  the cost  of facilities  required  to serve  new development:  Estimate  the
  total amount and the share  of the cost of planned  facilities  required  to accommodate
  new development;

  5.  Calculate  fee schedule:  Allocate facilities costs per  unit  of new  development  to
  calculate  the development  impact fee schedule;  and

  6.  Identify  alternative  funding  requirements:  Determine  if any  non-fee  funding  is
  required  to complete  projects.

The  key  public  policy  issue  in development  impact  fee  studies  is the  identification  of facility
standards  (step #2, above).  Facility standards  document  a reasonable  relationship between new
development  and the need  for new facilities. Standards  ensure that new development  does not
fund deficiencies  associated  with existing development.

Types  of Facility  Standards
There  are three separate  components  of facility  standards:

  *  Demand  standards  determine  the amount  of facilities  required  to accommodate  growth,
  for example,  park acres per thousand  residents,  square feet of library space per capita,
  or gallons of water per day. Demand standards  may also reflect a level of service such as
  the vehicle volume-to-capacity  (V/C) ratio used in traffic planning.

 3. Traffic  Facilities
This  chapter  summarizes  an  analysis  of  the  need  for  various  traffic  improvements  to
accommodate  new development.  The essential  nexus for this facility category  is between  the
demand  for new traffic facilities  from the projected  increase  in vehicle trips and the additional
traffic facilities  needed to meet  those service demands.  The fees are roughly  proportional  to
demand because they ensure that new development  will pay no more than its proportionate  share
of the identified planned facilities needed to serve the City through the planning horizon, and the
fees are scaled based on the number trips generated  by residential and nonresidential  land uses.
Impact fees will not fund the entirety of the identified facilities and the share of facilities needed to
serve existing development  must be funded with other funding sources. Fees implemented  at the
maximum  justified  rates would  allow  the City to maximize  use of other funding  sources  for other
purposes.

Nexus  Analysis  Summary
Traffic  fees in this report  are calculated  as follows:

  1.  Trip demand factors are identified to reflect'varying  levels of demand for trajfic facilities,
  by land use. The trip demand factors take vehicle  trip generation  rates, trip lengths and
  trip purpose into account.

  2.  Estimates  of current and projected  development  identified in Chapter 2 are multiplied by
  the trip demand factors to estimate current demand and projected for traffic facilities. The
  difference  between  current demana. and demand at the pla,nning horizon is assumed  to
  be new development's  share of total 'trip demand.

  3.  Capacity  expanding  projects  and  corresponding  costs  are  identified  from  the  City's
  various planning documents.

  4.  The cost of  the identified  :projects is allocated to new development,  based  on
  development's  share of trip demand at the planning horizon, calculated in Step 2.

  5.  The cost of planned'facilities  allocated  to new development  are divided  by the growth  in
  trip demand to calculate 'the cost per trip.

  6.  The cost per trip is multiplied  by the trip demand  factors  to determine  a fee, by land use.

Trip  Demand
The need for traffic facilities is based on the trip demand placed on the system by development.  A
reasonable  measure of demand is the number of average daily vehicle trips, adjusted for pass-by
trips. Vehicle trip generation  rates are a reasonable  measure or demand on the City's system of
traffic facilities across all modes because  alternate  modes (transit,  bicycle,  pedestrian)  often
substitute for vehicle trips. Pass-by trips are deducted  from the trip generation  rate. Pass-by trips
are intermediate  stops between an origin and a final destination  that require  no diversion  from the
route, such as stopping to get gas on the way to work.
